title: Gulf Allies Lose Faith in Trump as Iran War Drags On, Report Says
text:
Gulf Allies Lose Faith in Trump as Iran War Drags On, Report Says"

""

"Excerpt from Trump's Meeting with a Regional Ally"

"Gulf leaders are growing increasingly frustrated with the Trump administration's handling of the war with Iran, fearing that Washington lacks the diplomatic capability to secure a peace deal, according to a new report by The Washington Post."

"The report, cited by multiple Iranian media outlets, reveals that Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, and Bahrain have reached a shared concern over U.S. policy after months of conflict and continued Iranian missile and drone strikes."

"**"Trump started this war, and we are paying the price,"** a Gulf official told The Washington Post on condition of anonymity. According to the official, Arab anger toward the United States has now reached its highest level since the joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran in February."

"The frustration stems from Trump's contradictory approach—repeatedly threatening Iran with renewed strikes while simultaneously backing off and touting progress in negotiations. This inconsistency has led some Gulf countries to question whether hosting large U.S. military bases on their soil remains worthwhile."

"**"From the very beginning, there was dissatisfaction,"** said Firas Mqsd, Director of the Middle East and North Africa at the Eurasia Group. He noted that America's Gulf allies feel they have been **"dragged into a war for no reason"** —one that Trump is now struggling to end. Trump's Iran policy, he added, is often described in the region as **"unstable"** and **"unpredictable"**."

"**Trust in the United States has declined since the war began,** said Anna Jacobs, a researcher at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington. She added that U.S. allies believe Washington's actions have made them **"less secure, not more secure"**."

"While Gulf states still rely on the U.S. as their primary security partner and arms supplier, some are exploring alternatives. A recent mutual defense agreement among Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan was interpreted by a senior European official as **"a message to America"** —signaling that three powerful Sunni nations are **"trying to diversify their security and defense partnerships"** because **"America alone is no longer enough"**."

"The White House pushed back, insisting that Trump has **"excellent relationships with all our Gulf partners"** and that the U.S. has been in regular contact with regional allies."

"But analysts say the shift is real. The economic pressure from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, and the prolonged war have all deepened Gulf anxieties. Arab officials who once hoped for a quick end to the conflict are now demanding a resolution as soon as possible."

"Based on reporting from The Washington Post, as cited by Euronews Persian and Tasnim News Agency
